the free‐energy prediction errors in the mutation scan of the neurotensin‐1 receptor can be reduced by increasing sampling time and by using a consensus force field.
the free‐energy prediction error of the first principles of thermodynamics is reduced to 1.1 kcal mol−1 for a mutation scan of 762 amino‐acid changes in 12 proteins.

In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of an efficient and accurate approach for estimating changes in protein stability and protein–protein interaction energies, which is of particular interest for the rational protein design and engineering of biotechnologically relevant proteins.
the accurate prediction of the effects of single mutations in proteins, which are important for protein design and engineering, and for a better understanding of proteins.

the accurate prediction of the changes in protein free energies in a large‐scale mutation scan, which is of particular interest for the fields of protein engineering, biotechnology, bioengineering, and drug design.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the free‐energy prediction of proteins has reached a level of accuracy that matches the precision of experiments, and the remaining errors in the free‐energies are mostly due to experimental uncertainty and force‐field inaccuracy.
, with the current force‐field and the current sampling, the free energies are predicted with a standard deviation of about 0.5 kcal mol−1, which is comparable to the experimental error.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, with a combination of increased sampling and a consensus force‐ field approach, it is possible to achieve an accuracy of free‐energy predictions that is close to the experimental accuracy.
, with a consensus force field and increased sampling time, the remaining sources of error can be reduced to a level at which the accuracy of the predictions matches that of the experimental data.
the first principles of thermodynamics, together with a consensus approach, enable accurate free‐energy prediction in proteins.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, with the current state of affairs, we are close to being able to accurately predict the changes in protein thermodinamics upon mutation, provided that the sampling is increased.

, by combining a rigorous statistical‐mechanical approach with a consensus force‐ﬁeld approach, we are able to achieve a remarkable accuracy in the prediction of protein stability and protein binding.
, in principle, the accuracy of free‐energy predictions for proteins is not limited by sampling, but by force‐field accuracy and experimental error.
